title: Let nothing disturb thee
hook: a short poem found in her breviary: all things pass, God does not change, God alone suffices

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh rooms, spiritual marriage at the center of the castle. Your line was martha and mary together. Did you stop for three breaths before a job? Today, our last day with Teresa, and nine short lines. Day two hundred fifty-three.

Most of us have a scrap of paper we've kept longer than it deserves. A note in a wallet. A line taped inside a cabinet. A verse on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror. Something short enough to read with your toothbrush in your mouth, and strong enough to get you through the day. Teresa of Ávila had one too. Tradition says that after she died in 1582, the sisters found it tucked in her breviary, the prayer book she carried every day. Nine lines. People have been copying them ever since. Today's word is its first line.
screen: `A SCRAP OF PAPER YOU KEEP.` → `TUCKED IN HER PRAYER BOOK.` → `NINE LINES.`

segments.voice: In Teresa's Spanish, it begins: "Nada te turbe, nada te espante." Let nothing disturb you, nothing frighten you. The old English version begins, let nothing disturb thee. First, the worry. Teresa is not writing from a quiet life. She's writing from lawsuits, sickness, travel on broken roads, officials who tried to shut down her convents. These lines aren't a greeting card. They're what a busy, often frightened woman told herself. Second, what passes. The next lines say: everything passes. God does not change. Your worry, your triumph, your bad week, the officials who hate you, all of it passes. Only one thing stays still. Third, patience. Then: patience obtains everything. Not quick results. Patience. The kind of steady waiting she learned over a lifetime of prayer. Fourth, enough. And the ending, the part people carve on walls and stitch on cushions: whoever has God lacks nothing. And the last three words in Spanish: "Sólo Dios basta." God alone is enough. Here's what that doesn't mean. It doesn't mean Teresa didn't need friends, food or sleep. She loved her friends fiercely and wrote them hundreds of letters. It means that underneath everything, when all of it shakes, there is a floor. For Teresa, that floor had a name. A week ago we walked through her castle door. Tomorrow, her little friend, John of the Cross, whom she loved and teased.
screen: `WRITTEN FROM A HARD LIFE.` · `ALL THINGS PASS. GOD DOES NOT.` · `PATIENCE OBTAINS EVERYTHING.` · `WHOEVER HAS GOD LACKS NOTHING.` · then, large: `SÓLO DIOS BASTA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write it on a card. Find a scrap of paper, a sticky note, anything. Write the first line, let nothing disturb thee, or the last, God alone is enough. Then hold it and breathe. Think of one thing that's disturbing you right now. Read the line to it. If you pray, you can pray Teresa's lines as she did. If you don't, let the words steady you. Put the card where you'll see it tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Let nothing disturb thee. The first line of Teresa's nine-line poem, said to have been found in her breviary: all things pass, God does not change, God alone is enough. Today's word.
Your line: god alone is enough. Today, when something shakes you, read your card before you react. Day two hundred fifty-three. Teresa's castle, done. Tomorrow, John of the Cross.

howItsDone: Many Catholics keep Teresa's Nada te turbe on a prayer card or say it in hard moments, and it is sung around the world as a short, repeated chant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm saying for a calm life.
what it means: nine lines a busy, often frightened woman kept close: all things pass, God does not, God is enough.
what a scholar hears: the poem is known as Teresa's bookmark; the old English version is Longfellow's, 'let nothing disturb thee.'

notes: The Spanish lines ('Nada te turbe, / nada te espante', 'Sólo Dios basta') are quoted from the original; confirm spelling and accents. Middle lines (todo se pasa, Dios no se muda, la paciencia todo lo alcanza, quien a Dios tiene nada le falta) are rendered in English paraphrase.
The breviary discovery is tradition; stated as 'tradition says'.
Longfellow's translation ('Let nothing disturb thee…') is 19th-century and public domain but not on the validator's list, so it isn't quoted beyond the index title.
Teresa died in October 1582 at Alba de Tormes; confirm.
